newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil seen tightening by sector to cut trade gap.
newsitem.headline: Brazil seen tightening by sector to cut trade gap.

text.p: Bureaucrats may deny it, but the market is almost sure the Brazilian government is about to clamp credit restrictions on selected industries to reduce the country's runaway trade deficit.
"Credit restrictions are on the way," said Mauro Schneider, an economist at ING Barings in Brazil.
Despite recent attempts to boost exports and last month's restrictions on import financing, Brazil's 1997 trade outlook continues to be frightening.
In the first quarter of this year, Brazil posted a $3.06 billion trade deficit -- against a record $5.5 billion trade gap for all of 1996.
Early consensus estimates saw Brazil posting a $10 billion deficit in 1997. Now economists say that unless some action is taken to stem imports, those forecasts will be dramatically boosted.

On Friday, a published National Financial Institutions Association (ANDIMA) survey that showed half of the 15 banks polled believed the trade deficit would come in between $7 and $9 billion this year, as the economy grows 4.1 percent.
That mix of acceptable trade and growth would not require any significant change in forex or trade policy, the banks said.
But the other half of the banks surveyed said the economy is already overheating, and that if action is not taken, the trade deficit could rocket to $12 billion by the end of the year.
Senior government officials have repeatedly said there is no clear need for tighter monetary policy, as economic strength varies from sector to sector.
However, for the first time on Friday, Finance Minister Pedro Malan left economists wondering whether something is in the works. Asked if credit restrictions were on the way, Malan was ambiguous.
"You always ask me in such a way that I'm obliged to say no," he told reporters in Brasilia.
He then added: "If something in the future shows that we need to adopt measures, we won't avoid them."
Economists believe government action could be designed to yank in sectors that are galloping ahead: in particular, durable goods consumption, seen as the crux of the yawning trade gap.

"The government must make use of the instruments it has at hand," said Odair Abate, chief economist at Lloyds Bank Brazil, referring to credit restrictions. "That doesn't mean triggering a recession. The measures could be quite soft."
Abate said the government could move to slow consumption in determined sectors, like durable and semi-durable goods, such as electronic goods, automobiles and beverages.
However, he said it was important that something be done soon.
"(The government) should make a decision as soon as possible," Abate said. "The results of this kind of measure don't come overnight."

With credit restrictions, the government would also win time to reduce the so-called "Brazil Cost," the added costs of doing business in Brazil, and create conditions for sustained export growth, analysts said.
